Of the six in the fray for the MMRCA contract, two are from the US — the Lockheed Martin F-16 and the Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet — while the French are offering the omnirole Rafale fighter which has already been chosen by their air force as the future mainstay. The other contenders are the Saab Gripen from Sweden, the Eurofighter Typhoon and the Russian MiG-35.

As they await an Indian decision on the bids, Dassault Aviation and avionics major Thales, responsible for the design and development of the Rafale, have for the first time expressed a sense of unease over the format of the MMRCA request for proposal (RFP), pointing to the "gross mismatch" between the types of aircraft in the fray.

Officials of the two firms say "it's like comparing apples and oranges" — the Saab Gripen and F-16 are single-engine fighters while the Rafale, which is a multi-role aircraft, has two engines.

"The Rafale is a a twin-engine, heavier aircraft and in the same class as the Super Hornet and the Typhoon. The other three aircraft are of lighter variety. The India RFP, in the first analysis, is not extremely demanding but the IAF has to decide whether it wants a heavy or a light aircraft. We are worried, we don't want a situation where the other three are RFP compliant but we lose out on the price differential," J P H P Chabriol, senior vice-president of Dassault Aviation and responsible for military sales in Asia, Africa and America, told a group of visiting Indian journalists.

Similar fears were expressed by Francois Quentin, senior vice-president of Thales Aerospace Division, and Pierre-Yves Chaltiel, CEO of Thales Airborne Systems, though both said they were very hopeful that the Rafale would make the cut. "India has to decide whether it is looking at numbers or operational capabilities of the aircraft it thinks will meet its future needs," said Chaltiel. Quentin said they were counting on the "very happy Indian experience" with the Mirage 2000 — the Rafale is from the same stable, though a generation ahead — to secure the India contract.

Officials declined to reveal the unit price for a Rafale saying "that can be discussed once India decides on the RFP" but it is estimated that a single fighter could cost anything between $60 million and $90 million.

But it is the operational capabilities of the Rafale that is keeping French hopes alive for the MMRCA contract. Briefing reporters at the French Air Force base in St Dizier, Rafale pilots said the fighter can be used simultaneously for both air combat and ground attack missions, a capability which allows the use of fewer machines to achieve desired results.

In March 2007, the Rafale was deployed for the first time in combat operations in Afghanistan, flying out of Kandahar as part of coalition forces. Though there were no air-to-air missions to test its capabilities — the Taliban have no air force — the Rafale carried out laser-guided bombing missions in support of NATO ground troops.

The French Navy was the first to make the Rafale operational in June 2004, deploying it on the carrier Charles de Gaulle. Exactly two years later, the French Air Force made its first Rafale squadron operational for air defence and precision strikes. The aircraft relies on state-of-the-art equipment, its data fusion system allowing a pilot to quickly build up a tactical picture, identify targets in the air and on the ground and engage them from a stand-off position with precision weapons. There is no primary sensor on the Rafale — the electronic scanning radar, the front sector optronics, the Spectra electronic warfare suite and a secure datalink ensure situational awareness to the hilt. The Spectra system and 'low observable' airframe allow the Rafale to fly virtually undetected through air defence networks.

On board the Rafale are a wide range of passive sensors and missiles — the front sector optronics and the MBDA's infrared-guided Mica IR missile allow totally silent interceptions. The aircraft can be equipped with a range of missiles, precision-guided weapons and fuel tanks. For autonomous air operations, it can be equipped with a buddy-buddy refuelling pod under the fuselage and four external drop tanks under the wings — This gives the strike force an embedded in-flight refuelling capacity.

Dassault Aviation and Thales officials hope to build on the recognised track record of the Mirage 2000 — there are currently 51 Mirage 2000 at the IAF base in Gwalior and the French say they are ready to upgrade these to the standards of Mirage 2000-5 if India gives the go-ahead — and make a case for the Rafale in the IAF. The Rafale, though it has already been "combat proven" in the heat and dust of Afghanistan, will be brought to India next year and put through tests over the deserts of Rajasthan, in freezing Ladakh and humid Bangalore.

"The aircraft is very reliable, easy to maintain and repair — less than 30 per cent what it takes on a Mirage 2000. We believe the Rafale should be the natural choice for India after its Mirage 2000 experience," said a French Air Force pilot.

(The reporter is in France as part of a media group invited by Thales)

Heading: Tigresses elude team, Sariska relocation put off - Indian Express
Content:
In what could prove to be a major embarrassment for the Indian establishment, an assessment by a US Air Force (USAF) pilot who participated in the Red Flag joint exercise in Nevada in August claims that the SU 30 MKI, India's most modern aircraft, performed poorly in comparison with its US counterparts. The Su 30 MKI was outshone by US Air Force pilots and lost in one on one aerial combat with the older generation F 15 fighters, the review which was put up on a video sharing website last week, claims.

While the USAF officer in the video has not been identified, he appears to be a combat pilot of the rank of Colonel. He says that the Indian pilots suffered from a high fratricide rate, the term used for friendly kills, and had problems with the Sukhoi engines that were vulnerable to foreign object damage.

However, the Indian Air Force (IAF) said that the Sukhoi's held their own against ace pilots of the USAF and maintained a high serviceability rate throughout the exercise. For the record, the IAF has not commented on the outcome of the Red Flag exercise. "Out pilots were functioning on a stand-alone basis while the USAF pilots were part of a network and were getting inputs on navigation, target information and enemy details. We were getting all our inputs manually and were fighting fit even against all these odds," a top IAF officer said.

The USAF pilot says that the much touted thrust vectoring system of the Su 30 MKI's, which gives the fighter a high degree of agility in close aerial combat was also beaten by F 15 pilots who used their combat experience with the F 22 Raptors to find a flaw in the Indian fighter. Explaining the manoeuver in detail, the pilot says that the USAF tapped a vulnerability in the thrust vectoring system but the Indian pilots would soon find a way of rectifying the flaw.

Senior IAF officers however say that SU 30 MKI pilots were more than a match for their US counterparts and were fighting against all odds even when the French team was grounded for most of the time during the exercise.

"The US pilots at Red Flag were the best of their lot. From out side, a regular squadron with a mix of experienced and new pilots had gone. Above that, the US forces were part of a network and were even getting feedback from space assets," a senior officer said. He added that the Sukhoi's had the best serviceability record at the exercise and spent more time in the air than their French and South Korean counterparts. "We had a serviceability rate of above 90 percent. There is no question of foreign object damage to the engines. We had a tyre burst on the runway but it was changed within minutes by our ground crew," the officer said.

India marked it first-ever presence in the prestigious Red Flag exercise and crossed swords with the the French Air Force (with Rafale fighters), South Korean Air Force (with F-15s) and the US Air Force with their F-15s and F-16s. IAF, which participating with eight Su-30s, two IL-78 tankers an IL-76 aircraft, spent close to Rs 100 crore on the exercise, termed as the world's toughest aerial combat exercise.

Heading: Broadcasters resort to reruns as TV shoots stalled again - Indian Express
Content:
Four days, a 12-member expert team, darting and trapping equipment, signals from two radio collars on two tigresses, a customised cage, a truck, and a specially flown in MI-17 IAF helicopter from Rajasthan's Jodhpur unit patiently waiting on stand-by.

Despite the glut of technology, the combined strength of the Wildlife Institute of India, the Rajasthan Forest Department, and the National Tiger Conservation Authority could not capture even one of the two collared tigresses in Ranthambhore for translocation to a new home and habitat in Sariska. On November 6, four days after the official translocation deadline of November 3, the exercise was officially abandoned. It will be resumed about a week later, or more specifically, as and when the tigress is more accessible.

The translocation attempt is part of the Rs 1.5-crore plan to shift two tigers and three tigresses from Ranthambhore to Sariska, which lost all its tigers to poachers. In July-August, a tiger pair was successfully translocated.

Subsequently, two more tigresses were radio-collared to be moved later. But both have eluded the expert team which captured the first pair. Among those in the team are WII Director P R Sinha, WII experts Parag Nigam and K Sankar, Rajasthan Chief Wildlife Warden R N Mehrotra and Rajasthan Special Empowered Committee member Rajpal Singh. The original date set for the translocation was November 3. But as forest staff, including Park Director G Somashekhar, waited in Sariska, word came in around noon that the trapping team was near a tigress which hadn't made a kill that day. The team did not want to tranquilise her as she hadn't eaten. The exercise was put off for the next day.

But on the second day, the tigress moved away, covering a lot of ground. WII officials were informed that the second collared tigress should not be touched as she was in the tourist zone.

Day 3, the first tigress had made its way to the Sawai Mansingh sanctuary, situated on the periphery of Ranthambhore, hiding in deep thickets. While the team knew the tigress's location, they could not get the cage — or their own vehicle — to her as the area is inaccessible. The other tigress's signal was almost gone.

On the fourth day, November 6, the tigress did not emerge at any suitable location. The team decided to wrap up and leave Ranthambhore. One WII researcher has been stationed there to monitor the movements of the tigress.

Heading: ‘Scared of being Scarlett II’ - Indian Express
Content:
In what is turning out to be the worst ever phase in the Indian television industry, all channels stopped airing original programming from Sunday. This implies that no fresh episodes of shows produced locally will be aired, with the exception of Bigg Boss, and the channels will telecast only reruns. The decision was announced at a press conference attended by the various channel heads on Monday evening.

The decision closely follows the letter dated October 30, issued jointly by the broadcasters — INX Media, Star India, Sahara One Media and Entertainment, Viacom18 Media and NDTV Imagine — to the various producers' associations. The letter said the channels refuse to increase production budgets and appealed to cine workers and producers to resume normalcy in work by November 9. Any failure in doing so, the letter said, would result in reruns of all shows thereon. Bigg Boss, however, is an exception for two reasons: the format of the show does not accommodate any such modifications and there are only ten more days for the show to end, said the statement issued by the broadcasters at the meet.

The problem between the producers and cine workers has been on for over a month now. On October 1, cine workers went on a four-day strike, which ended after a resolution to reconsider wages was reached. However, the arrangement didn't last long and the last week had producers shooting only two hours of primetime content while other shows went on reruns.

Heading: India awaits nuke-submarine mishap report, short delay in induction likely - Indian Express
Content:
Justifying the withdrawal of complaint against a high profile minister's son whom she accused of raping her minor daughter, the German mother said she was afraid that her daughter may become "Scarlett II".

"Since the day I have filed the complaint on October 14, life has become hell for both me and my daughter. We are also scared of being Scarlett II," reads the letter written and submitted by the German mother on Sunday afternoon.

The letter had sought to withdraw her complaint against Rohit, son of Goa Education Minister Atanasio Monserratte. The mother had complained that Rohit had raped her daughter. The police had booked Rohit based on the complaint. He was arrested almost a month after the complaint was filed.

Scarlett, mentioned in the letter, is a British teenager who was found dead on Goa's popular Anjuna Beach on February 18.

In the letter, the German mother has claimed that they were in a state of shock and depression and were scared of proceeding with the case, especially after the murderous attack on her counsel Aires Rodrigues, on the night before she was to formally register her complaint before a senior police officer.

"We have learnt the bitter truth, that making genuine complaints against the rich and mighty is entirely counter productive. We are constantly hounded, our names sullied, campaigns organised against us and all sorts of motives attributed to us," the letter reads.

Heading: PM wraps up Gulf visit with security, investment deal - Indian Express
Content:
India is awaiting a formal report on the Russian 'Nerpa' Akula II class nuclear attack submarine accident that left 21 sailors dead on Saturday evening even as top officials have confirmed that its induction into the Indian Navy is not likely to be delayed by more than a few months given the minimal damage suffered by the vessel.

While Russia has ordered a board of inquiry into the gas leak that took place when the Nerpa was undergoing sea trials off Vladivostok, top Navy officers in India say that the vessel did not suffer any structural or reactor damage and the induction would at most be delayed by two months if no major flaw is detected.

The Navy will wait for a formal report on the incident after the completion of the board of inquiry but initial inputs here suggest that the accident could have most likely taken place due to a human error given that a large number of dockyard technicians were on board for the sea trials.

"The accident took place when more than 200 personnel were on board the vessel. Shipyard technicians would not be trained to handle such emergencies and the gas leak could have happened due to the accidental pressing of a lever or failure of a safeguard mechanism," a senior officer said.

Naval experts who are familiar with the functioning of the Russian Navy say the only thing that could delay the eventual clearance of the submarine for induction would be the board of inquiry.

"There will be thorough board of inquiry as people have died in the accident. That will have its own implications. They will have to question a lot of people and that will take time (before the vessel is cleared). However, the submarine made it back to port on its own power and there are no reports of damage to the reactor," Vice-Admiral (retd) A K Singh, who has commanded INS Chakra, India's sole nuclear submarine that was leased from Russia in 1988, told The Indian Express.

The official reaction of the Russian Navy to the accident too indicates that the gas leak could have happened due to a human error. "The statement of 'unauthorised activation' of the fire fighting system implies that the gas leak was done accidentally. The system starves the compartments of oxygen that could have caused death by suffocation," the officer, who retired as the Flag Officer Commanding in Chief of the Eastern Command, said.

Meanwhile, India will shortly take a call on whether to send its personnel for training to Russia on the submarine. With reports indicating that the vessel will not be sailing for at least a few weeks, the Navy will have to decide whether the first batch of 40 personnel who were to train on the submarine would leave New Delhi this week.

Heading: At V-Cs meet, OBC quota takes centrestage, SC orders awaited - Indian Express
Content:
Prime Minister Manmohan Singh on Monday wrapped up his maiden visit to the Gulf on a successful note that saw him inking agreements for defence cooperation with Qatar and investments with Oman, and more crucially making a pitch for stepping up energy imports.

The highlight of the November 8-10, two-nation visit was the signing of defence and security cooperation agreement with Qatar that lays the framework for collaboration on maritime security, sharing intelligence and information on extremist threats, money laundering and smuggling of narcotics. "The agreement is just short of stationing troops (in the region)," a top Indian official said.

India also sought an additional 5 million tons of liquefied natural gas from Qatar to meet its growing energy needs and has proposed to set up a gas-fired fertiliser plant in the Gulf nation to meets its urea needs. "We had an excellent one-hour meeting. (Qatar's Deputy Prime Minister Abdullah bin Hamad al) Attiyah is a great friend of India and promised to look into our LNG needs," Petroleum Minister Murli Deora said.

Within hours of Singh's arrival in Doha, agreements on defence and security cooperation were signed. Joint training exercises, training of personnel and maritime cooperation were highlights of the defence pact signed by Defence Secretary Vijay Singh and his Qatari counterpart last evening after Singh held delegation level talks with his counterpart Jabor al Thani. Another pact on law and security enforcement deals with money laundering and transnational crimes. It lays out the framework for sharing information and database on threats posed by extremists, and other security and legal matters.

Heading: L&T gets nod for Mumbai monorail - Indian Express
Content:
Even as the HRD Ministry issued directions last month to all Central Educational institutions (CEIs) to fill up all vacant OBC seats in this academic session itself, the issue has raised a lot of concern among heads of these institutes with academic sessions running mid way through their course now. At the vice-chancellors' conference in New Delhi on Monday, the issue was discussed and further action would depend on the apex court's directions on re-opening of admissions, expected at next week's hearing.

The Supreme Court had said last month that vacant seats should go to the general category students if there are no eligible OBC quota students and this exercise should preferably be completed by October-end.

HRD Minister Arjun Singh meanwhile, said at the conference that efforts should be made to enable the minority communities to be equal partners in shaping the country's future.

"We have to gear ourselves to deliver to the minority communities in India to enable them to become equal partners in shaping the country's future. Unless all people in the country feel they have space to exist and flourish, the purpose of education is not served," he said.

Singh, who once said the higher education was a sick child, on Monday said the sector had shown signs of vigour now. "It is no more a sick child. Prime Minister has been extending all help for the growth of higher education in the country."

On the issue of filling quota seats, which occupied a whole lot of discussion space at the conference, the HRD Ministry said in a presentation that while 8,240 seats were earmarked for OBC candidates in 24 central universities (CUs), only about 5,599 seats have been filled up so far. While the highest vacancies are at Delhi University that has 2,023 of the 2,389 reserved seats lying vacant, Banaras Hindu University has 109 vacant seats, 76 in Hyderabad University 76 and and JNU 29. A few thousand reserved seats are lying vacant at CEIs taken together.

Things are better off in the technical educational institutes. Additional Secretary Ashok Thakur said only 23 seats are lying vacant in OBC category in the old IITs, while there is no vacancy in the OBC segment in IIMs. In the new IITs, which started functioning from this academic year, 66 OBC seats are lying vacant. The seats meant for Schedules Caste (SC) and Scheduled Tribe (ST) students have been filled up in all the IITs, he said. However, in IIMs, 13.23 per cent seats have been filled by SC students against their quota of 15 per cent. Similarly 5.62 per cent seats have gone to ST students against their quota of 7.5 per cent.

"The court had said the seats should be preferably filled up by October-end as per the rules and regulations.The upper limit of creamy layer, which has been kept out of quota ambit, has been increased from Rs 2.5 lakh to Rs 4.5 lakh. Given all these issues, we are waiting for the direction of the court," a senior HRD official said.

Heading: In regime change,Maldives palace to become varsity - Indian Express
Content:
The Mumbai Metropolitan Regional Development Authority (MMRDA) has formally handed over the Letter of Agreement (LOA) to the consortium led by Larsen & Toubro with Scomi Engineering, a Malaysia-based company, to build the country's first monorail.

The consortium had bagged the contract for the monorail project, from Jacob Circle to Chembur via Wadala, on October 10 but had not received the LOA.

With the LOA being handed over, the work on the monorail is expected to start by January. The monorail project is to being built on a Design-Build-Operate-Transfer (DBOT) basis and is expected to cost around Rs 2,460 crore.

As per the design prepared by the consortium, 18 stations are expected on the 20 km route. The 'straddle' type monorail will not connect the island city to suburbs, but would provide interconnectivity to the existing suburban railway (Mahalaxmi and Lower Parel stations of Western Railway, Curry Road, Dadar and Wadala stations of Central Railway) and forthcoming Metro Rail as part of multimodal transport system.

As per the agreement, the project has to be competed within 30 months. Of this, the first phase (from Jacob Circle to Wadala) would be fully operational in 24 months while the second phase (from Wadala to Chembur via Mahul) would be operational in next 6 months. Earlier, apart from Larsen & Toubro and Scomi, a consortium led by Reliance Infrastructure with Hitachi (Japan) and Canada-based Bombardier had been short-listed for the project.

Heading: Britain lifts ban on civilian nuclear exports to India - Indian Express
Content:
As Male's main boulevard gets ready -- with red-and-green flags of Mohamed Nasheed Anni's party -- for the new dawn on Tuesday when their beloved leader takes over as the new President of Maldives, streets are abuzz with Anni's announcement that he will be converting Gayoom's presidential palace into this tiny nation's first university.

Many consider it populist, many say it's symbolic. But nobody, be it young or old, rich or poor, questions its need in this country which doesn't have a single degree-awarding college so far.

Gayoom's presidential palace has a white façade, with tall gates and a lawn separating the gate with the main porch -- this two-storeyed mansion is clearly the biggest residence in Male, which is characterised by narrow and congested lanes. Some say it has a swimming pool, and there are estimates in the local media that the palace cost $62 million to build.

"This is Anni's promise that he will not stay there in the palatial mansion. We badly need higher education institution in this country," says Hameed, who owns a fleet of ferries in the Male jetty. Perhaps, Nasheed, who himself studied maritime studies at John Moores University in Liverpool (UK), knows it better than anyone else.

Although literacy rate, according to the 2006 stats, is 93.83 per cent in Maldives and even English is widely spoken by the Maldivians, its educational institutions offer only O level and A level courses in its country according to the Cambridge curriculum.

"As a result, people who can afford and want to study, go abroad. The most popular destinations are UK, Singapore, Malaysia and Trivandrum," says Rasheeq Suleimani, who runs a shop of garments in downtown Male.

While this is a noble move, say most in Male, they also regard this as the "ultimate anti-establishment" move against the previous Gayoom administration, which had charged Nasheed on 27 grounds and jailed 13 times. Anni is believed to have spent a total of six years in the Dhoonidhoo jail, meant for the political prisoners.

Nasheed, or Anni, who was named as the "prisoner of conscience" by the Amnesty International in 1996 and is even dubbed as the "Mandela of the Maldives", is able to excite the youngsters and gain respect of the elderly alike.

Many still question his unproven experience, or his largely untested administrative acumen in the Government but no one is able to challenge his integrity so far. "That is because he has never held power under the Gayoom Government, unlike most of his party leaders who have done so and then defected to Anni's party," says N Sathiyamoorthy, director of Observer Research Foundation, Chennai, who has come all the way to Male to witness the oath-taking ceremony.

Heading: The Alva Echo - Indian Express
Content:
In a significant development, Britain on Monday said it has lifted a six-year-long ban on export of sensitive nuclear technology to India for civilian purpose.

"Since March 2002 UK policy has been to refuse all licence applications for Trigger List items to India," Foreign Office Minister Bill Rammell said. "That policy has now changed and we will now consider on a case by case basis licence applications for peaceful use of all items on the NSG Trigger List and NSG Dual-Use List when they are destined for IAEA safeguarded civil nuclear facilities in India," Rammell told the House of Commons in a written statement. Firms had been barred from supplying equipment and material on the Nuclear Suppliers Group "trigger list" to India since 2002 but the change in the Government's position follows an NSG statement in September allowing an exemption from the group's guidelines for civil nuclear facilities which are safeguarded by the IAEA.

The ban will remain in force on items destined for "unsafeguarded nuclear fuel cycle or nuclear explosive activities" or where there is an "unacceptable risk" the material might be diverted to those activities. "We will continue to encourage contacts between UK nuclear scientists, academics and those working in or with the UK nuclear industry with their Indian counterparts, except where we consider that such contacts might be of assistance to the weapons-related aspects of its nuclear programme.

Heading: BJP Govt failed to implement schemes: Rahul - Indian Express
Content:
In a bid to embarrass the Congress, the ruling BJP has sought to make AICC general secretary Margaret Alva's outburst against her own party an election issue.

"Woh chunawi ticket bechte hai, ham garibo ko sasta chawal (They sell election tickets, we give rice to the poor at subsidised prices)," says a BJP advertisement released in local newspapers across Chhattisgarh.

The BJP has also prepared CDs of Alva's allegation that the Congress had picked candidates in the Karnataka assembly elections in exchange for money. "Let the people know how the century-old party selects its candidates for elections", says BJP leader Ravi Shankar Prasad, in charge of the state during polls. "The people of Chhattisgarh have a right to know whether the Congress candidates in the state had also paid for their tickets".

State Congress spokesman Amir Ali Faristha has sought to ridicule the BJP's attempt to make Alva's remark its campaign issue. Leaders of the saffron party have been involved in the largest number of scams in the past, he claims.

Heading: How many corners in Chhattisgarh? - Indian Express
Content:
AICC general secretary Rahul Gandhi on Monday accused the BJP Government in Chhattisgarh of failing to properly implement the Centrally-sponsored schemes and said that its benefits did not percolate to the needy because of the corruption prevalent in the state.

"The UPA Government has ensured that this state received more funds than it got during the previous NDA regime, but it did not reach the masses," he said at election meetings held at Jagdalpur and Bhilai Steel City. "The NDA government used to send Rs 800 crore to the state four years ago. Now, it has increased to Rs 8,000 crore, registering a 10-fold increase," he claimed. Recalling Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi's associations with the region, he said both these leaders had taken steps for the uplift of tribals and weaker sections of society.

Heading: Dholakia’s film may resume shooting in January - Indian Express
Content:
As Chhattisgarh heads to polls in two phases next week to elect its 90 member Assembly, the contest appears evenly poised between the BJP and the Congress. While other political parties are struggling to make their presence felt in this bi-polar state, vote shares of both the BJP and the Congress in the last two elections — one held when it was part of undivided Madhya Pradesh and then after formation of a separate state in 2000 — indicate that the coming contest is heading for a sharp finish.

In the 1998 Assembly polls, held before the creation of the state, the difference in vote share between the Congress and BJP in Chhattisgarh region was just 0.56 per cent. At the time of the state's formation, the Congress had 48 members in the assembly while the BJP had 36, the BSP had three and the Gondwana Gantantra Party had one member.

In the new state's maiden polls held in December 2003, the BJP wrested power from the Congress by securing 39.26 per cent of the vote and 50 seats. The Congress polled 36.71 per cent of the vote and won 37 seats. The BSP won two seats and the NCP bagged a seat. A marginal swing of 2.55 per cent marred Congress prospects, therefore, enabling the BJP to form the government.

Looking back, the Congress suffered a major setback following erosion of its so-called tribal vote bank as well as due to the NCP, which played spoilsport by securing 7.02 per cent of the vote. However, the NCP could win only one seat. This time, the Congress has struck a seat sharing arrangement with the NCP. In spite of its efforts to emerge as a balancing factor, the BSP won only two seats in 2003, securing 4.45 per cent of the vote.

Battling the dreaded anti-incumbency factor, the ruling BJP has adopted the 'Gujarat formula' to deny tickets to 14 of its sitting legislators and has introduced new faces in 46 constituencies. The Congress has largely relied on candidates with experience. "Where is the anti-incumbency factor at state level? It could be only at the local level." Chief Minister Raman Singh told The Indian Express.

At the same time, in an attempt to ape Narendra Modi's style and success in the Gujarat Assembly polls last year, Raman Singh declares at every poll meeting that "The BJP candidate is in front of you. In fact, Raman Singh himself is contesting from all the 90 constituencies. When you elect the BJP candidate, you are selecting me".

"Raman cannot become Modi. The Gujarat style will not work here", counters the Congress's Ajit Jogi who is leading the campaign for his party. "Modi linked himself with Gujarat's pride but that's not the case with Raman Singh", he says.

Chhattisgarh's tribal population holds the key to power in the state as it constitutes about 32 per cent of the entire population. While 29 seats are reserved for the tribals, both the BJP and the Congress have fielded 32 tribal candidates each. The state's Scheduled Caste population is 12 per cent and the Other Backward Classes (OBC) form 52 per cent.

The Bahujan Samaj Party has fielded its candidates from all 90 constituencies, mimicking its Uttar Pradesh formula of giving tickets to upper castes as well. In turn, both the BJP and the Congress have given the maximum number of tickets to OBC candidates: The BJP gave 28 tickets to OBCs while Congress nominated 21 candidates belonging to this section.

While the BJP has not fielded any candidate from the Muslim minority, the Congress has attempted a balance by fielding candidates from the Christian, Muslim, and Sikh communities. Both parties have given 10 tickets each to women candidates.

Political observers point out that the caste factor has not dominated the overall outcome of polls in this region. It has been known to play a crucial role in particular constituencies, however — for instance, in areas where the OBC Sahu community, which constitutes 15 per cent of the backward classes, and the SC Satnami community has a strong presence.

The new state confronts old problems such as large-scale migration of agricultural labourers every year, slow pace of development in the education and health sectors. But none of these issues are set to dominate the poll scene in this election.

The Naxalite issue and the controversial anti-Naxal movement, Salwa Judum, is being discussed only in the tribal Bastar region where the Maoist rebels are active.

Chief Minister Raman Singh claims that 'development' is the only poll issue before the people. Poll watchers say that the ruling BJP's electioneering so far is similar to the saffron party's famous 'India Shining' campaign during the last Lok Sabha polls. On the other hand, the opposition Congress is highlighting the alleged corruption during the BJP regime. "Decentralisation of corruption is a major achievement of BJP government which has devised innovative methods for it", says state Congress working president Satya Narain Sharma.

The battlelines are being drawn between the Congress and BJP in this bipolar state. But chances are, should either the Congress or BJP fail to secure a majority, in the event of a hung assembly, the CPI and BSP could emerge as power centres in the post-poll scenario in Chhattisgarh.

Heading: J&K poll boycott campaign gets a boost, Mirwaiz says will hit streets - Indian Express
Content:
The shooting of Rahul Dholakia's film Lamha, which has been disrupted thrice since the crew arrived in Kashmir a month back, will start again in January when the unit will return to Srinagar, hopefully with Bipasha Basu.

The unit intends to shoot only the vital scenes of the movie in the Valley as the most part of the film has already been shot on a set in Film City in Mumbai.

Bipasha Basu, who was shooting for the film at Anantnag on Wednesday, left the shoot midway after the locals created a ruckus on the set. This forced the entire crew, including co-star Sanjay Dutt, to follow her out of Kashmir.

"We can't understand why she left suddenly when things were going smoothly," said Bunty Walia, the producer of the film. "We're sure she had her reasons. And we're fully convinced that she'll return to Srinagar in January and complete the unfinished work," Walia said.

"I hope they will come back in January," said Farooq Shah, director, Tourism. "It is good for our tourism industry. Bollywood gives us good publicity and I hope many more directors will come to Kashmir to shoot their films," he added.

Shooting of Lamha had to be halted earlier on two occasions, first when fruit traders in Srinagar objected to a scene showing guns being packed in apple boxes, and then after objections were raised by students of a college in Anantnag to some of the portions of the film being shot inside their college premises.

Heading: Alva finds support in senior leader - Indian Express
Content:
The separatist poll boycott call in Jammu and Kashmir got a new lease of life on Monday with Hurriyat moderate leader Mirwaiz Umar Farooq announcing that he would hit the streets as part of the protest.

Mirwaiz asked mainstream politicians on Monday to stay away from the elections or face social boycott.

Although Mirwaiz and his moderate Hurriyat had earlier supported the poll boycott, he has kept away from roadside protests. The Government too has refrained from arresting him even as all the hardline Hurriyat leaders, several senior moderate leaders and JKLF chief Yasin Malik were detained and booked under the Public Safety Act along with 70 other leaders in a crackdown ahead of the polls.

However, Mirwaiz is now ready to step up his boycott campaign. "On November 14, I will myself go to Bandipore and organise an (anti-election) public rally there," he said. "We will not succumb to any pressure."

Incidentally, Mirwaiz's decision to make himself more visible in the election boycott campaign coincides with the return of hardliner Syed Ali Geelani to the Valley after surgery in Delhi. Soon after his return, on November 14, Geelani will start his boycott campaign from Srinagar.

The Hurriyat chairman also announced a joint anti-poll programme by the Kashmir Coordination Committee — an amalgam of various separatist constituents — including peaceful marches to district headquarters on voting days. He reiterated that on December 24, when the eight Assembly segments in Srinagar district go to polls, they will hold a march to Lal Chowk.

On election days, people will first assemble at district headquarters and then march to tehsil headquarters and stage sit-ins outside polling booths. "The people will march to the United Nations office to submit a memorandum and then spread out to different Assembly constituencies of Srinagar," Mirwaiz said. The Hurriyat leader also called for a blackout in the evenings on poll days.

However, he stressed on peaceful protests. "There should be no violence... Nobody will be allowed to pelt stones on (security) forces or government buildings."

Mirwaiz questioned statements by mainstream politicians that elections can't affect the Kashmir dispute and are purely for administrative purposes. "The elections can't be a substitute to the right for self-determination. We appeal to spirited people to stay away from the so-called election process at this crucial and decisive juncture," he said.

Heading: A Lone against the boycott - Indian Express
Content:
Within an hour of the Congress rubbishing AICC general secretary Margaret Alva's allegation of sale of party tickets, senior party leader Yogendra Makwana, who heads the Scheduled Caste cell of the AICC, came out in her support. Makwana, who was a Union minister during Indira Gandhi's regime, claimed he had also got complaints from two candidates seeking tickets for the Rajasthan Assembly elections. While a woman aspirant seeking a ticket from Baran was asked to pay Rs 80 lakh, another in Alwar was asked to pay Rs 40 lakh, he claimed.

"They said some tout called Sharma had made the demand. I asked them to complain to the Congress president. There should be an inquiry into Margaret Alva's allegations," Makwana told reporters.

"People also talk about a coterie around the Congress president," he added.

The party's SC cell head also questioned why none of the 30 names recommended by him for tickets had been accepted. "What is the need for this department if its recommendations are not needed?," he said.

Makwana added that he was not bothered about any disciplinary action because he was speaking the "truth", and asserted that he was thinking of resigning from the party as he was "feeling suffocated".

Makwana's support to Alva came after AICC spokesperson Jayanthi Natarajan clarified at a press briefing that there would be no probe into the Congress leader's allegations as they were "baseless".

Natarajan even contradicted AICC media cell chairperson M Veerappa Moily, who has gone on record saying that Alva's case had been referred to the party's Disciplinary Action Committee.

Heading: Asna case accused killed ‘making bomb’ - Indian Express
Content:
Poll fervour may be missing in the Valley but Shabnum Lone has plunged into the electoral fray. Her decision pits her against her brothers Sajjad and Bilal Lone and the party of their father, Abdul Gani Lone, who was assassinated seven years ago. Shabnum Lone, a senior lawyer and the older sister of the Lone brothers, is contesting from Kupwara, a stronghold of the People's Conference, a separatist political party founded by her late father.

In a way, the Lone family has become the microcosm of Kashmir's complicated political discourse.While Shabnum is contesting the elections, her brothers, especially Sajjad Lone, ardently advocate a poll boycott. Sajjad Lone, in fact, has given a call for a march against elections in north Kashmir from November 12; the government has already put him under house arrest.

The politics of the Lone brothers and their sister seeks to draw upon the capital accumulated by their late father who was one of the most respected political figures of Kashmir. But their respective interpretations of the Lone legacy are so much at odds that they have divided the family and split the siblings.

When contacted, Shabnum Lone said that the decision to contest polls was not entirely taken by her. "People from Kupwara came to my house on October 24, pleading with me to contest. It is my father's lifelong investment and they (the people) honour, love and revere him," she said. "They came to me and I had no choice but to return to my home to fight for them".

When asked how her decision to contest polls will play especially at a time when her brothers are at the forefront of the boycott campaign, she said "I do believe that we are adults and educated and entitled to take our own decisions. Like I have a right to contest elections, they have a right to boycott it¿ I believe that elections are not a solution to Kashmir issue. This dispute has to be resolved between the governments of India and Pakistan and people of Kashmir." But "at the same time, there are so many other issues which cannot wait till the Kashmir dispute is resolved. There are real human stories which are untold, stories of abject poverty, discrimination and day to day problems. I want to bring them forward and help the people".

Though Shabnum Lone has decided to go against her brothers and the People's Conference now, the estranged relations between the siblings is not news in these parts. The Lone family had split earlier too when the People's Conference was divided between the Lone brothers. The Hurriyat Conference was divided on the issue of the stand taken by Sajjad Lone against Pakistan and Hurriyat hardliner Syed Ali Shah Geelani after Abdul Gani Lone's assassination by militants on May 21, 2001 and the subsequent proxy participation by the People's Conference in the 2002 assembly polls. The Lone brothers went with the moderate camp led by Mirwaiz Umar Farooq and finally split when Sajjad parted ways with the separatist conglomerate while Bilal continued to remain with the Hurriyat moderates. The brothers, however, reunited soon after even though Sajjad didn't re-enter the Hurriyat.

Heading: Saravana owner’s son faces life ban on entering US - Indian Express
Content:
Eight years ago, five-year-old Asna's name had seared itself into Kerala's conscience when she had joined the list of innocent victims of Kannur's cycle of mindless political violence. One of the six accused in the crude bomb attack that claimed Asna's right leg was a 20-year-old youth, Cheruvancheri Pradeepan.

Four days before a verdict was to come in the case, Kannur's bloody history caught up with Pradeepan. Out on bail, he was blown apart today morning while allegedly assembling a bomb with another RSS accomplice, Dileesh, who was also killed.

The scattered remains of the two 28-year-olds were gathered from the premises of a temple at Cheruvancheri in Kannur, where a traditional folk festival was held last night. Both were natives of Cheruvancheri.

RSS Kannur district karyavahak T Sajeevan claimed the blast occurred when they were packing stuff brought for fireworks at the temple. The fireworks did not take place as the temple committee opposed it on religious grounds, he said. Sajeevan could not explain why the RSS men had brought the explosive materials then.

Earlier too, BJP and CPI(M) members have lost their lives while assembling bombs in the state, and Cheruvanchery — a Sangh Parivar territory — is not new to political violence.

The police are working on two theories. The bomb-making could have been part of the routine piling of weapons and explosives in Kannur around this time for another bout of bloodletting. Both Sangh Parivar and CPI(M) camps are bracing themselves up for death anniversaries of their martyrs.

Another theory is related to the session's court verdict on the bomb attack on Asna, who was also a native of Cheruvanchery. The attack on Asna happened on September 27, 2000, during the time of election to local bodies in the state. She was playing in front of her grandfather's house when RSS men hurled bombs; their target apparently were Congress activists suspected to be hiding in her house.

RSS men might have been preparing for an attack if the court verdict was against them, sources believe.

Heading: Rebel Communists in Kerala to form a political outfit - Indian Express
Content:
Arrested on charges of human trafficking made by the US Consulate here, the Managing Director of the Saravana Bhavan Group of Hotels, P R Shivakumar, could face a life-long ban on entering the US. The 36-year-old Shivakumar, the son of the owner of the popular South Indian eatery chain, was looking after its overseas business and is accused of sending employees to the US on forged documents. He has been remanded to 15 days' judicial custody by a city court and will be grilled by the Crime Branch-CID over the coming days.

The Saravana Group operates 25 hotels in India and another 22 overseas, including the US, UK and Singapore.

Asked about the possibility of a life ban on Shivakumar, Bryan W Dalton, US Consul and Chief of Consular Services, told reporters here on Monday that depending on the nature of the violation, Shivakumar could be barred entry to America for periods ranging between five years and a lifetime.

According to officials at the Consulate office here, Shivakumar had tried to send four cooks to their outlet in the US in the guise of "production executives" and produced forged documents during the visa interview. The accused, say officials, were trying to circumvent US rules that do not allow cooks to seek work visa.

Though their application claimed that they were skilled persons en route to attend an international fair on food packaging and processing held in Chicago between November 8-14, it was found that the four — A Gurusamy, S Arumugam, Ramu Murugaiyyan and Sekar Kannayiram — had little or no knowledge of the technology. The documents that the accused presented even had a recommendation from the Chennai chapter of the Indo-American Chamber of Commerce.

Following this, the Assistant Regional Security Officer of the Consulate, Anthony K Ramirez, filed a complaint with the CB-CID, requesting immediate action against the group.

Shivakumar and Ramu Murugaiyyan were arrested on Sunday on charges of cheating and forgery, while hunt is on for the other three. Police officials added that they recovered documents related to the fraud from the corporate office of the hotel group in Chennai. Consulate officials have also cancelled the contract signed with the hotel after the development.

According to police sources, investigations are also on to determine if the group had used fake documents earlier too for the same purpose. Senior officials of the Tamil Nadu Police said they were also looking into all such operations of hotel chains involved in business overseas.

This is the latest scandal to hit the Saravana Group family. Earlier Shivakumar's father Rajagopal, who started the chain as a small eatery 27 years ago, was convicted in the murder of one of his employees, Santhakumar, in 2001.

Heading: Nun told to come for identification - Indian Express
Content:
The scattered Communist rebel outfits that have been gnawing into several CPI(M) bastions in the state are all set to regroup themselves into a state-level political movement. The rebel plank wants to cash in on the growing disenchantment with the CPI(M) leadership. Last year, the expelled CPI(M) leaders had formed the Communist Campaign Committee (CCC), for spearheading the ideological struggle. The CCC would also merge into the common political body, contours of which will be finalised before the next Lok Sabha poll.

In the recent months, many local and area-level leaders owing allegiance to Chief Minister V S Achuthanandan had been expelled from the party, controlled by state secretary Pinarayi Vijayan.

The ousted leaders have formed parallel Communist forums in their respective turfs and have stormed into many CPI(M) strongholds in Kozhikode, Palakkad and Thrissur districts. Even certain local committees in Kannur, the party's cradle and hometown of Pinarayi and PB member Kodiyeri Balakrishnan, have shown tangible symptoms of evolving the rebel movement.

"The ongoing revolt is against the ideological bankruptcy and moral turpitude nagging the present CPI(M) leadership. Those who have opposed the wrong policies of the leadership have been thrown out," said a rebel leader, closely associated with the state-level platform.

A common trait of the rebel forums is their mass support. The promptness of the party rank and file in identifying with the issues raised by the rebels indicates the resentment brewing within the party. Provocations for local and area-level mutinies range from corruptions to faction politics.

The party has been ticking over with office-bearers at Onchiyam, Ottapalam, Kunnamangalam, Mavoor, Atholy and Shornur in north Kerala where rebels have ensured a firm grip over party base. The Communist history of Onchiyam in Kozhikode district could be traced back to pre-Independence days. Despite desperate attempts, Pinarayi could not wean away the Onchiyam comrades who have formed a local Marxist party. To make matters worse for the party, the upsurge is fast spreading into other areas. The party leadership is at a loss to tackle this grassroots-level rebellion. The sword of discipline seemed to be ineffective as the movement is mass in nature rather than a leader-centric.

"Had the dissidence been triggered by a leader, the party could have stemmed the trend by ejecting him out. Disciplinary action would not serve any purpose as the present issue has to be addressed at the bottom-level," said a CPI(M) leader of the official faction.

According to sources, VS has become submissive due to various compulsions. But his followers want to carry forward the struggle he had launched against the right-wing deviation of a section in the party.

Heading: Last overs - Indian Express
Content:
A Kandhamal district court on Monday asked the 29-year-old Catholic nun, who was allegedly raped on August 25, to attend identification parade of the accused persons at Baliguda on November 19.

The nun, who after initial hesitations had agreed to cooperate with the police in the rape probe, on Monday informed the court that she could not attend the identification parade as she was undergoing trauma counselling in Kerala.

Though her lawyer Manas Singh sought a month's time, Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate of Baliguda, Dolagobinda Barik rejected the plea and instead asked her to attend the parade on November 19. The victim in her petition to the court had urged that the parade be held in Delhi between November 17 and 19.

The court, however, remained silent on the nun's request for change of venue for the parade and said the exercise would be conducted at Baliguda within its jurisdiction.

The police had lined up the 10 arrested in the case as well as 100 others who were part of the mob that allegedly humiliated her on August 25.

Heading: The audacity of restraint - Indian Express
Content:
Sometimes the apt gesture is about more than one person's sense of occasion. After Australia's ninth wicket fell on Monday afternoon, Mahendra Singh Dhoni gave control of proceedings to Sourav Ganguly. From a current skipper to a former one on his last day of Test cricket, it was a touching gesture. It was also a nod to the game, its players and its audiences, an unarticulated desire to see Ganguly as we will remember him, the man in charge, most often for better but sometimes for worse. And so the Nagpur Test ended thus: the man who presided over India's longest winning streaks was notionally in charge of a spectacular victory moment. It was also such a Ganguly moment. Master of the off-side, maverick strategist, groomer of lost young cricketers, he also possessed an instinct and a flair for drama. Good then that he did not retire quietly to the Nagpur dressing room, even after the Bradman-esque spectacle of a last innings duck. It was also, to the day, eight years since he captained his first Test.

More than Ganguly's cricket, it was his drama that divided his audiences into camps, with the division always very porous. Sometimes it was awesome. Those centuries on Test debut. That mastery of the off-side. Those clean sixes over long-on. But always he appeared to be aware of the occasion. He hinted as much in a recent interview. After the trauma of being dropped without being given much of a chance on an Australian tour, he said he suspected that second chances would not come his way again soon, he had to prove himself on that Lord's debut. He did, with a century and some wickets, following it up with a consecutive century. That would be his way of grooming India out of the desolation of the lost '90s, a decade of indifferent cricket and matchfixing scandals. To be counted, the Indian team had to perform. To perform, his young hopes — most prominently, Harbhajan Singh — had to be given enough chances to make good. To give themselves a chance, India had to match up to the best, harnessing professional support staff, learning to enjoy themselves on tour, steeling themselves for competitive aggression, especially against the Australians.

We'll miss Ganguly. In retirement, after a last series when it finally went so right for him, we'll probably find that memories of the darker side, the pettier side even, of his drama will fade, and those of his enthrallingly successful captaincy of India burnished.

Heading: Declaration of intent - Indian Express
Content:
Honeymoons, by definition, don't last long. Recognising this iron law, US President-elect Barack Obama has begun to cover his flank by lowering expectations. In his victory speech last week, he cautioned American people against setbacks and false starts amidst the very difficult challenges that confront his presidency — "two wars, a planet in peril, the worst financial crisis in a century".

During the campaign, Obama's political genius lay in avoiding detail and presenting a large blank slate that others could write on. Running for office, however, is not the same as governing from it.

On the domestic front, Obama refused to be defined as a liberal Democrat, who might tax and spend his way through the next four years. He has in fact promised a tax cut for the middle classes, a sacrilege from the perspective of the Democratic Party's left. On social issues too, Obama has sought to bridge the deep divide between liberals and conservatives in America.

On the external front, however, his pronouncements have been closer to the liberal internationalist view that dominates the Democratic Party's foreign policy establishment. Obama can emerge a statesman on the world stage, if he can resist the activist temptations of American liberal internationalism and choose instead strategic restraint as the over-arching theme of his foreign policy.

A number of factors demand American restraint today. One, Obama faces constraints on the conduct of American foreign policy that no post-American president had to cope with. His emphasis, then, must be on the domestic — the renewal of American national strength.

Two, despite the outpouring of goodwill for him across the world, Obama will not find it easy to make nice to the world. There is no doubt that many of President George

W. Bush's policies made America unpopular around the world. That does not necessarily mean that the world's resentments against America started with Bush and will end with his departure from the White House. Anti-Americanism has been an enduring world wide phenomenon since the '60s.

Just recall the so-called "golden age" of Bill Clinton. It was one of America's European allies, France, that referred to Clinton's America as a "hyperpower" during the '90s. If Bush's Iraq intervention was attacked as illegitimate, so was Clinton's war in Kosovo by Russia, China and many others. Neither of them had the mandate of the United Nations Security Council.

If Bush has been criticised for short-circuiting the UN, many in the third world attacked Clinton for using the UN Security Council to undermine the concept of national sovereignty in the name of "humanitarian intervention". Whether America rejects the UN or embraces it, there will be objections.

Put simply, power breeds resentment. So long as it remains the sole superpower, America's actions, irrespective of intent, will always generate suspicion.

Three, the limits on the use of American power are real and Obama will pay dearly if he ignores this like Bush. After the Cold War the US establishment believed it had the freedom to pursue any external goal it chose. The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan have proven otherwise. Yet there is nothing to suggest that the liberal internationalists have grasped this lesson.

Like the much-reviled neo-conservatives, the liberal internationalists too believe that American power can and must be deployed to achieve specific political objectives. If Bush gambled on Iraq, Obama's liberals are rearing to have a go at Sudan and "save" its Darfur region. "Arrogance of power" is a trait that afflicts America's liberal internationalists as acutely as it does the neo-conservatives.

Fourth, the negative consequences of recent American adventurism around the world should tell Obama that doing less might actually mean more for the US. But the liberal internationalists, who will populate the next administration, are getting ready to pursue their favourite lost causes.

The arms controllers want an early implementation of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty and negotiate a universal moratorium on the production of fissile materials. Some of them want to abolish nuclear weapons altogether. The list goes on from building peace in West Asia to resolving the Kashmir dispute, from rejuvenating multilateralism to rebuilding failed states.

Leadership is about defining priorities. Those who try to do everything achieve nothing. Given the current US preoccupation in Iraq and Afghanistan, it is unlikely if the US has the resources and energy to chase the whole laundry list of the world's problems.

Fifth, leadership is about delegation. An America that sheds many of its secondary burdens will be better placed to shape the larger security architecture of the world. An America that cuts some geopolitical slack to other powers and acts as the balancer among them will create more options for itself. If the US continues to jump in first everywhere, Obama will invite as much resentment as Bush did.

Finally, despite his lack of foreign policy experience, Obama should trust his own judgments rather than the conventional wisdom of American liberal internationalism, and its many single-issue groups who are bound to spread American power thin.

The one original proposition that Obama took during the campaign was the hint of direct US talks with Iran. Under pressure from the liberals of his own party, who tend to be even more hawkish on Iran than the Republicans, Obama did add caveats.

That he held on to the essence of the argument that America must talk even to its enemies, despite the political controversy it generated, suggests Obama may be willing to rethink many entrenched but self-defeating American foreign policy positions. That surely offers some hope.

The writer is a professor at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore

Heading: No-no-confidence - Indian Express
Content:
Seizing the initiative in these troubled times, the Jamiat Ulema-e-Hind expressed a consensus condemning terrorism as un-Islamic. More than 6000 clerics signed the declaration, and reminded the nation that jihad and terrorism were "poles apart" and that "terrorism is the biggest crime as per the Quran". What's more, they displayed a grown-up refusal to play politics over revelations about Hindu militants arrested in connection with the recent bomb blasts, saying that terrorism should not be linked to any religion.

They also pressed for a separate law to deal with communal violence, and greater representation of Muslims in education and employment. Certainly, the Jamiat Ulema-e-Hind's resolution carries great moral weight and legitimacy among Indian Muslim communities, and the resolution is a sensible move away from victimhood to agency. It is a welcome attempt at reaching out to the rest of the nation and carving a moderate space to respond to the particular exigencies of the situation facing those communities.

Unfortunately, the entire spectrum of commentators that conflate Islam and terrorist activity and suggest that the religion encourages a willed surrender of independent thinking fail to recognise how any religion shape-shifts in response to changing situations. Jihad itself is a normative concept in the Quran, an ethical mission and a warlike one — variously deployed depending on political circumstance — and the Hyderabad resolution clearly distinguished between the two.

"Jihad is a constructive phenomenon and a fundamental right of human beings whereas terrorism is based on destruction", said the statement. For instance, scholars of the Deoband movement have pointed out politics is a matter of pragmatic response for them, and that they function best in secular regimes that allow them the autonomy to prescribe "correct practice". So like the Darul Uloom's similar statement in May, the Hyderabad fatwa is another encouraging demonstration of the tugs within the ulema. In the nervous dysfunctional environment following terrorist attacks, this fatwa fits in with the impulse of protecting their flock as well as underlining religion's bedrock of shared peace.

Heading: Imaginary numbers - Indian Express
Content:
In the midst of threats to withdraw support to the ruling coalition at the Centre, the UPA government somehow believes that by refusing to prorogue the Lok Sabha, it can deny the opportunity to the opposition to test the strength of the government on the floor. The Supreme Court had long back held in the Bommai case that the house floor is the only place where the majority is tested. The principle laid down by the Supreme Court does nothing but reiterate Article 75 (3) of the Indian Constitution, which states that the council of ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. The court only fixed the venue for the test; it did not invent any new principle.

Unlike testing the majority, which can be done only on the floor, raising the question of whether a government commands a majority need not be raised only on the floor, through a no-confidence motion or otherwise. The opposition has every right to raise this question anywhere outside the House, and, in times of defections and instability, sometimes often — so long as the government's majority is not in doubt. It is the responsibility of the conscience-keepers of the Constitution, and particularly of the president of India, to address those doubts of the opposition that can be considered justified by directing the cabinet to seek the vote of confidence on the floor. Thus, the right of the opposition to question the government's majority does not depend on whether Parliament is in session or not; any belief that non-prorogation of the House stymies the opposition from raising it on the floor is unsustainable.

The current session of the lower house — the 14th session of the 14th Lok Sabha — commenced on July 12, 2008. The government moved a vote of confidence on July 21; the next day, the vote was won amidst well-remembered scenes of controversy. (A special committee of the Lok Sabha is still investigating the controversy.) Meanwhile, political parties have issued threats of withdrawing support to the governing coalition. The session which was adjourned sine die by the speaker on July 22 was not prorogued as used to be the parliamentary practice and tradition, but reconvened as Part II of the 14th session on October 17. That was done in the false belief and hope that the then opposition would not be able to table another no-confidence motion against the government; the belief was that if the House was reconvened as Part II of the same session, Rule 338 of the Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha would come into play. The rule says that a motion shall not raise a question substantially identical with one on which the house has given a decision in the same session.

Applying the rule, Speaker G.S. Dhillon disallowed a motion on September 4, 1974, tabled by Madhu Limaye on the grounds that a no-confidence motion tabled by Jyoti Basu against Indira Gandhi was already discussed and negatived on July 23 in the same session. Yet no rule, regulating in-house procedure in the Lok Sabha, made as it is in exercise of powers under article 118 of the Constitution, can supersede the grand constitutional postulate in Article 75(3) — which gives the opposition the right, invaluable in a parliamentary democracy, to try to unseat any government for want of majority. Using Rule 338 to abridge the right to table no-confidence motions when the government needs to be unseated for want of majority is surely ultra vires the Constitution. Either the meaning of the rule needs to be revised or a rider should be added it should not apply to constitutionally-enabled motions like no-confidence motions. Otherwise, a no-confidence motion defeated at the beginning of a session, cannot be tabled at a later time in the same session, even when the government has visibly lost majority.

We may feel that this is acceptable in this instance. But consider where it leads. In the fast-declining political culture of our country, is it so unbelievable to imagine a chief minister, with a fragile majority — and a collusive governor and a friendly Central government — summoning the first session of a new House, winning a vote and then keeping it running into many parts over its entire tenure to escape accountability on the floor?

The writer is the secretary of the Goa Legislative Assembly & author of many books on parliamentary procedure
